title: Tesla's Missing Autopilot Data Showed It Detected A Hazard Before Fatal Crash, Despite Claims It Was Missing

reading.body:
A Tesla vehicle struck a parked car in March 2024, killing one person and injuring another. Tesla told the family and the court it had no crash data from the incident. A Russian hacker later recovered the data through Tesla's bug bounty program, proving the company possessed it all along. The recovered data showed Tesla's Autopilot had detected a hazard before the crash.

This is a failure of disclosure in litigation. Tesla made a factual assertion that data did not exist when it did, preventing the injured parties and court from accessing information central to understanding what the vehicle's system detected and how it responded. A jury found Tesla partially responsible in August 2025, and a judge upheld a verdict ordering the company to pay $243 million in damages. The failure was caught only because an independent security researcher probed Tesla's systems under its bug bounty program, not through Tesla's own processes or court discovery.

It is not established whether Tesla's initial claim of missing data resulted from poor data retention practices, a failure to search its systems thoroughly, or deliberate concealment.

summary:
Tesla faced a lawsuit after one of its self-driving vehicles struck a parked car in March 2024, killing Naibel Benavides Leon and injuring Dillon Angulo. A jury found Tesla partially responsible in August 2025, and a judge upheld the verdict in February 2026. Tesla was ordered to pay $243 million in damages and renamed its Autopilot and Full Self Driving features to clarify that human supervision is required. The company initially claimed it had no crash data from the incident, but a Russian hacker discovered that Tesla actually retained the information.

The hacker, working through Tesla's bug bounty program, recovered the missing crash data and proved the company possessed it all along. His evidence was crucial to the jury's decision against Tesla. Since then, Tesla has strengthened its crash data security. The case raises concerns as Elon Musk prepares to launch fully autonomous Cybercabs, especially given recent high-profile accidents involving Tesla's self-driving systems, including 207 crashes in May involving driver-assist features.
